title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: In the shed where Pierre was put, and where he stayed four weeks, there were twenty-three soldiers, three officers and two officials.

When Pierre remembered them later, they all seemed like misty figures, except Platon Karataev. Karataev stayed in his mind as a vivid and precious memory, the embodiment of everything Russian, kindly and round. When Pierre saw his neighbor at dawn the next morning, his first impression of something round was fully confirmed. Platon's whole figure was round — in a French overcoat tied with a cord, a soldier's cap and bast shoes. His head was perfectly round. So were his back, his chest, his shoulders and even his arms, which he held as if always ready to embrace something. His pleasant smile and his large, gentle brown eyes were round too.

Platon Karataev must have been about fifty, going by the campaigns he described in the manner of an old soldier. He did not know his own age and could not work it out. But when he laughed, which he often did, his strong, brilliantly white teeth showed in two unbroken semicircles, every one of them sound. There was not a gray hair in his beard or on his head, and his whole body gave an impression of suppleness and above all of firmness and endurance.

His face, though lined with fine, rounded wrinkles, looked innocent and young, and his voice was pleasant and musical. But the chief peculiarity of his speech was its directness and aptness. It was evident that he never thought about what he had said or was about to say, and so the quickness and rightness of his intonation carried an irresistible persuasiveness.

In the first days of his imprisonment he was so strong and nimble that he seemed not to know what tiredness or sickness meant. Every night before lying down he said, "Lord, lay me down like a stone and raise me up like a loaf!" and every morning when he got up he said, "I lay down and curled up, I get up and shake myself." And indeed, he only had to lie down to fall asleep like a stone, and he only had to shake himself to be ready for work at once, the way children are ready to play the moment they wake. He could do everything, not very well but not badly either. He baked, cooked, sewed, planed and mended boots. He was always busy, and only at night did he allow himself conversation, which he loved, and songs. He did not sing like a trained singer who knows he is being listened to. He sang like the birds, evidently letting the sounds out the way one stretches or walks about to get rid of stiffness. The sounds were always high, mournful, delicate and almost feminine, and his face was very serious while he sang.

Since being taken prisoner and letting his beard grow, he seemed to have shed everything that had been forced on him — everything military and foreign to himself — and gone back to his old peasant ways.
"A soldier on leave — a shirt outside breeches," he would say.

He did not like talking about his soldiering, though he never complained, and he often mentioned that in all his army service he had not been flogged once. When he told a story, it was usually some old and evidently precious memory of his "Christian" life, as he called his life as a peasant. His talk was full of proverbs, but they were mostly not the coarse, indecent sayings soldiers use. They were the kind of folk sayings that seem so insignificant when taken without a context, and then suddenly take on the force of profound wisdom when used at the right moment.

He would often say the exact opposite of what he had said on an earlier occasion, and yet both would be right. He liked to talk and he talked well, adorning his speech with endearments and with folk sayings that Pierre thought he made up himself. But the chief charm of his talk lay in the fact that the most ordinary events — sometimes the very ones Pierre had witnessed without noticing them — took on a character of solemn fitness in Karataev's telling. He liked to hear the folk tales that one of the soldiers told in the evenings (they were always the same), but most of all he liked to hear stories of real life. He would smile with joy as he listened to them, now and then putting in a word or asking a question to make the moral beauty of what he was told clear to himself. Karataev had no attachments, friendships or love, as Pierre understood them. But he loved everything life brought him in contact with, and lived affectionately with it, particularly with people — not any particular person, but whoever happened to be there. He loved his dog, his comrades, the French and Pierre, who was his neighbor. Yet Pierre felt that in spite of Karataev's affectionate tenderness toward him (by which he unconsciously gave Pierre's spiritual life its due), Karataev would not have grieved for a moment at parting from him. And Pierre began to feel the same way toward Karataev.

To all the other prisoners Platon Karataev seemed a perfectly ordinary soldier. They called him "little falcon" or "Platosha," teased him good-naturedly and sent him on errands. But to Pierre he always remained what he had seemed that first night: an unfathomable, rounded, eternal embodiment of the spirit of simplicity and truth.
Platon Karataev knew nothing by heart except his prayers. When he began to speak, he seemed not to know how he would finish.

Sometimes Pierre was struck by the meaning of his words and asked him to repeat them, but Platon could never recall what he had said a moment earlier. In the same way he could never repeat the words of his favorite song for Pierre. The words "native" and "birch tree" and "my heart is sick" occurred in it, but spoken rather than sung, it made no sense. He did not understand, and could not understand, the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the expression of an activity unknown to him, which was his life. But his life, as he saw it, had no meaning as a separate thing. It had meaning only as part of a whole of which he was always aware. His words and actions flowed from him as evenly, inevitably and spontaneously as fragrance comes from a flower. He could not understand the value or significance of any single word or deed taken by itself.
